questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the first step in the structured reading approach for a lifecycle scenario?
options: Immediately write the final answer before reading further
Identify what change is being proposed -- declarative or programmatic, which object/process, how many users affected
Assume every scenario is testing the same governance mechanism
Skip straight to naming a Salesforce feature by name
questions.explain: The four-step approach starts with identifying the nature of the proposed change itself, before moving on to lifecycle stage, the gap, and the specific mechanism that closes it.

questions.q: In Worked Scenario 1 (the Friday validation rule), what was the actual gap being tested?
options: Rollback planning and deployment-timing judgment -- there was no pre-approved rollback path or consideration of who'd be monitoring the change over the following two days
That validation rules should never be used on the Opportunity object
That sales reps are never allowed to enter placeholder data
That CAB approval is unnecessary for declarative changes
questions.explain: The scenario's gap was the missing rollback plan and a deployment-timing decision (Friday afternoon, no weekend monitoring) rather than anything wrong with validation rules as a concept.

questions.q: In Worked Scenario 2 (the duplicate custom object), why does this lesson say the CAB wasn't actually at fault for approving the deployment?
options: Because the CAB never actually approved anything in that scenario
Because the development team lied to the CAB about what they were building
Because CABs are not responsible for any approvals on custom objects
Because the CAB correctly judged the change safe to deploy -- a CAB evaluates deployment safety, not architectural fit, and the real missing step was an architecture review board at design time
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly distinguishes what a CAB evaluates (deployment safety) from what an architecture review board evaluates (design fit) -- the CAB did its actual job correctly; the gap was upstream.

questions.q: What makes Worked Scenario 3 (the conflicting Account updates) a metadata-conflict scenario rather than a code-quality scenario, per this lesson?
options: Both teams' automations were individually poorly tested
Only one of the two teams actually tested their automation

Both changes were individually sound and well-tested in isolation, but conflicted once deployed together because nobody had cross-team visibility or a shared release calendar to catch the overlap in advance
Salesforce does not allow two automations to touch the same object
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that neither team's individual testing would have caught this -- the gap was the missing shared calendar and cross-team visibility, exactly the Lesson 8 metadata-conflict pattern, not a quality defect in either automation.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why does the scenario-reasoning skill matter beyond passing any single exam?
options: It doesn't matter beyond exams -- it's purely a test-taking trick
Because reading for the actual gap and mapping it to the specific mechanism is the same discipline a real CAB or architecture review board meeting demands in the moment, not just a study technique
Because only Salesforce-certified architects are ever asked to analyze scenarios
Because scenario reasoning replaces the need for any technical knowledge at all
questions.explain: The lesson frames this as a transferable real-world skill -- the same reasoning habit is what an actual governance body needs in a live meeting, not just an exam-preparation exercise.
